module_title: Cider Making from Local Apples and Pears

lessons.title: Sourcing Apples and Pears in African Climates: Varieties and Seasons
lessons.body: In Africa, apples and pears grow best in cooler highland areas like the Kenyan Highlands, Ethiopian Highlands, and South African Cape. Varieties such as Anna, Golden Dorsett, and Granny Smith thrive in these regions. Pears like Packham's Triumph and Forelle also do well. If you're in a warmer area, look for low-chill varieties like 'Tropical Beauty' apple or 'Kieffer' pear. Harvest seasons vary: in South Africa, apples are picked from February to April; in Kenya, from December to February. For cider, you want a mix of sweet, tart, and bitter fruits. Sweet apples (e.g., Fuji) give sugar, tart apples (e.g., Granny Smith) give acidity, and bitter pears (e.g., wild pears) give tannins. Aim for a ratio of 60% sweet, 30% tart, 10% bitter. If you can't find bitter fruits, add black tea (for tannins) later. Buy directly from farms or markets during peak season when prices are low. Choose fully ripe, blemish-free fruit. Windfalls are okay but use them quickly and wash thoroughly. For a 20-liter batch of cider, you need about 15-20 kg of fruit. If fresh fruit is scarce, you can use unsweetened apple juice (not from concentrate) as a base, but fresh is better. In hot climates, fruit spoils fast, so press within 2-3 days of harvest. Store fruit in a cool, dark place. If you must delay, refrigerate. Remember, cider quality starts with fruit quality.

lessons.title: Crushing and Pressing: DIY Press from a Car Jack
lessons.body: You don't need expensive equipment to crush and press apples and pears. A simple DIY press can be built with a car jack, a wooden frame, and a bucket. First, crush the fruit. Use a clean, food-grade plastic bucket and a sturdy wooden pole (like a broom handle) to smash the fruit into a pulp. Alternatively, use a clean, new garbage disposal unit if you have electricity, but manual crushing works. For a 20-liter batch, you'll need about 20 kg of crushed fruit. Next, build the press: get a strong wooden frame (like a small table with a hole in the center) and a car jack (scissor or hydraulic). Place a mesh bag (nylon or cheesecloth) filled with pulp on a wooden pressing board with grooves to channel juice. Put another board on top, and use the jack to apply pressure slowly. Collect juice in a clean bucket below. Press in batches; don't overload. A 2-ton jack can press about 5 kg of pulp at a time. Yield: 20 kg of fruit gives roughly 12-15 liters of juice, depending on fruit type. Pears yield more juice than apples. After pressing, strain the juice through a fine mesh to remove solids. For better clarity, let it settle overnight and siphon off the clear juice. Sanitize all equipment with a solution of 1 tablespoon bleach per 4 liters of water, then rinse with boiled cooled water. Work quickly to avoid oxidation. In hot weather, add a campden tablet (1 per 4 liters) to kill wild yeast and bacteria before fermentation. If you don't have campden, use a starter culture of strong yeast to outcompete wild microbes. This DIY press costs less than $30 and can be reused.

lessons.title: Fermentation: Choosing Yeast for Dry or Sweet Cider
lessons.body: Fermentation turns sweet juice into cider. The yeast you choose determines whether your cider ends up dry or sweet. For dry cider, use a champagne yeast or wine yeast like EC-1118, which ferments all sugars, leaving little residual sweetness. For sweet cider, use an ale yeast like Safale S-04 or Nottingham, which leaves some sugars unfermented. Alternatively, you can back-sweeten after fermentation. Start by measuring the sugar content with a hydrometer. Ideal starting gravity for cider is 1.045 to 1.060. If lower, add sugar (1 kg per 20 liters raises gravity by about 0.020). Add yeast nutrient (1 teaspoon per 4 liters) to prevent stuck fermentation, especially in hot climates. Pitch yeast at a rate of 1 gram per 4 liters. Ferment in a food-grade bucket or carboy with an airlock. Keep temperature between 18-24Â°C. In hot weather, place the fermenter in a water bath with a wet towel to cool it. Fermentation takes 1-2 weeks. For dry cider, let it ferment until gravity reaches 1.000 or below. For sweet cider, stop fermentation at 1.010-1.015 by cold crashing (place in fridge for 2 days) and adding potassium sorbate (1/2 teaspoon per 4 liters) and campden tablet (1 per 4 liters) to stabilize. Then rack (siphon) into a clean container, leaving sediment behind. Taste and adjust: if too tart, add a little sugar syrup; if too sweet, add acid blend (1 teaspoon per 20 liters). Age for 2-4 weeks for better flavor. Always sanitize everything. In Africa, wild yeast can spoil your cider, so use commercial yeast for consistent results.

lessons.title: Secondary Fermentation and Carbonation in Bottles
lessons.body: Secondary fermentation clarifies cider and creates bubbles. After primary fermentation, rack your cider into a clean carboy, leaving behind the yeast cake. Fit an airlock and let it sit for 2-4 weeks at 18-22Â°C. This reduces off-flavors and drops more sediment. For carbonation, you have two options: bottle conditioning or forced carbonation. Bottle conditioning is simple: add priming sugar to the cider before bottling. Use 7-10 grams of sugar per liter of cider (about 1 teaspoon per 500ml bottle). Dissolve the sugar in a small amount of hot water, cool, and gently stir into the cider without splashing. Then fill sanitized bottles, leaving 2-3 cm headspace. Cap or cork. Store bottles at 18-24Â°C for 1-2 weeks to carbonate. In hot weather, carbonation happens faster, so check after 3-4 days by opening one bottle. If it's fizzy enough, move bottles to a cool place (10-15Â°C) to stop further fermentation. Be careful: too much sugar can cause bottle bombs. Use sturdy bottles (beer bottles or champagne bottles). For a drier cider, use less sugar; for sweeter, use more but stabilize first. If you prefer not to bottle condition, you can use a keg and CO2 tank, but that's expensive. Another method is to add a small amount of fresh juice to each bottle before capping, but that's less predictable. Always sanitize bottles and caps. After carbonation, let bottles condition for another 2 weeks for best flavor. Serve chilled. In Africa, where temperatures are high, store bottles in a cool dark place to avoid over-carbonation.

lessons.title: Flavoring with Ginger, Hibiscus, and Baobab
lessons.body: Adding local flavors makes your cider unique. Ginger, hibiscus, and baobab are widely available in Africa and add distinct tastes. For ginger cider, use fresh ginger: 50-100 grams per 20 liters, grated and boiled in 1 liter of water for 10 minutes, then cooled and added to secondary fermentation. This gives a spicy kick. Alternatively, add 1 teaspoon of ground ginger per 4 liters. For hibiscus (zobo) cider, use dried hibiscus petals: 100 grams per 20 liters, steeped in hot water for 20 minutes, strained, and added to secondary. This adds tartness and a deep red color. For baobab cider, use baobab fruit powder: 2-3 tablespoons per 20 liters, mixed into the cider before bottling. Baobab adds a citrusy, tangy flavor and is rich in vitamin C. When flavoring, always add to secondary fermentation or after stabilizing to avoid interfering with primary fermentation. If adding during primary, flavors may be muted. For best results, make a flavor extract: steep ingredients in a small amount of vodka or neutral spirit for 1 week, then add to taste. This avoids dilution and contamination. Start with small amounts; you can always add more. Taste after 3 days and adjust. For ginger, you can also add sliced ginger directly to bottles for a stronger bite, but be careful of over-carbonation. Hibiscus can inhibit yeast, so add after fermentation. Baobab powder is safe to add anytime. Remember to sanitize everything. These flavors not only improve taste but also use local ingredients, reducing costs and supporting local farmers. Experiment with ratios to suit your palate.

lessons.title: Preventing Oxidation and Spoilage in Hot Weather
lessons.body: Hot weather speeds up oxidation and spoilage. Oxidation makes cider taste like cardboard or sherry. To prevent it, minimize splashing when racking or bottling. Use a siphon hose that reaches the bottom of the container. Fill containers to the top to reduce headspace; if you can't, flush with CO2. Add campden tablets (1 per 4 liters) at each racking to scavenge oxygen. Spoilage from bacteria and wild yeast is also a risk. Always sanitize equipment with a no-rinse sanitizer like Star San (1 oz per 5 gallons) or bleach solution (1 tablespoon per 4 liters, then rinse). Keep fermenters sealed with airlocks. In hot climates, ferment at the low end of yeast's temperature range (18-20Â°C) by placing the fermenter in a cool box with ice packs or a wet towel. If temperature exceeds 25Â°C, off-flavors develop. For storage, keep bottles in a dark, cool place (10-15Â°C). If you don't have a cellar, use a refrigerator or a buried container. Add potassium metabisulfite (1/4 teaspoon per 20 liters) before bottling to prevent refermentation and oxidation. For sweet cider, add potassium sorbate (1/2 teaspoon per 4 liters) to stop yeast. If you see mold or smell vinegar, discard the batch. Vinegar flies are a sign of spoilage; keep containers covered. Use airlocks with sanitizer. In Africa, power outages can affect refrigeration, so plan ahead. Make smaller batches that you can consume quickly. Proper sanitation and oxygen management are key to long-lasting cider.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Cider Making from Local Apples and Pears

This practical reference consolidates the six core lessons of the RISE AFRICA module Cider Making from Local Apples and Pears into a single working document you can print, laminate and pin inside the production room. It is written for small-scale African cider makers who intend to sell, not just ferment. Every number, temperature and timing below is chosen because it protects product quality, shelf life and margin in hot climates where spoilage organisms work faster than they do in Europe or North America.

If you are producing cider for market in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Nigeria or Ghana, treat this as your operating manual. The business logic is simple: consistent, safe, shelf-stable cider commands repeat orders from bars, lodges, supermarkets and export buyers. Inconsistent cider destroys brand trust after one bad batch.

Data Table 1: Apple and Pear Selection Guide for African Climates

Variety / Type Region Suitability Harvest Window Cider Role Brix at Harvest Tannin / Acid Profile
Granny Smith South Africa, Zimbabwe, Kenya highlands MarâMay (SA), JunâAug (Kenya) Acid base 11â13 High malic acid, low tannin
Golden Delicious South Africa, Morocco, Egypt FebâApr (SA) Body / sugar 12â14 Low acid, low tannin
Anna / Dorsett Golden Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Zambia NovâJan (warm lowlands) Volume base 10â12 Moderate acid, low tannin
Cripps Pink (Pink Lady) South Africa, Kenya highlands AprâJun (SA) Premium single-variety 13â15 Balanced acid, light tannin
Local crab apples Throughout Africa where present Varies, often OctâDec Tannin / structure 9â12 High tannin, high acid
Packham's Triumph (pear) South Africa, Kenya, Zimbabwe FebâApr (SA) Perry base 12â14 Low acid, low tannin, high sorbitol
Forelle (pear) South Africa FebâMar Perry aroma 11â13 Moderate acid, aromatic

Sources: South African Apple and Pear Producers' Association (SAAPPA) annual harvest reports; Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO) fruit variety bulletins; FAO FAOSTAT crop calendars for East and Southern Africa.

Data Table 2: Fermentation, Carbonation and Storage Parameters

Stage Parameter Target Range African Climate Adjustment Business Impact
Juice prep pH 3.2â3.8 Add malic acid if pH > 4.0 Prevents spoilage, extends shelf life
Juice prep Brix (OG) 11â14 Â°Bx Chaptalise with cane sugar if < 10 Â°Bx Hits 4.5â6.5% ABV target
Primary fermentation Temperature 18â24Â°C Use wet cloth / evaporative cooling above 26Â°C Preserves fruity esters, avoids fusel alcohols
Primary fermentation Duration 7â14 days Shorten if ambient > 28Â°C Faster cash cycle
Yeast choice Strain Nottingham / SafCider / EC-1118 EC-1118 for hot climates (18â30Â°C tolerant) Predictable attenuation
Secondary fermentation Priming sugar 5â8 g/L Reduce to 4â5 g/L above 28Â°C Prevents bottle bombs
Bottle conditioning Temperature 18â22Â°C Never exceed 25Â°C Controls COâ pressure
Bottle conditioning Duration 10â14 days Check at day 7 in hot weather Avoids over-carbonation
Storage Temperature 12â18Â°C Shade + ventilation; no direct sun Slows oxidation and refermentation
Storage Shelf life (unopened) 6â12 months 3â6 months above 25Â°C Inventory turnover planning

Sources: Lallemand Cider & Perry Yeast Handbook; Fermentis SafCider technical data sheets; ASBC Methods of Analysis for titratable acidity and ABV determination.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Bottle Bombs and Explosive Carbonation

Never bottle cider before primary fermentation has fully finished (stable gravity reading for 3 consecutive days). In African ambient temperatures above 28Â°C, residual sugar plus priming sugar can over-carbonate within 48 hours and shatter glass bottles, causing serious eye and facial injuries.

  • Always use pressure-rated glass bottles (champagne or flip-top), never thin beverage bottles.
  • Wear safety glasses and gloves during bottling and while opening conditioned bottles.
  • Store conditioning bottles inside a closed plastic crate or wooden box, never loose on a shelf.
  • If a bottle shows bulging crown cap, visible sediment ring high on the neck, or hissing on gentle cap pressure, chill it immediately in a covered container and open outdoors, away from people.
  • Do not use PET soda bottles as a substitute unless you are prepared to monitor firmness daily and refrigerate once firm.

Flavouring with Local Botanicals

Ginger, hibiscus (roselle) and baobab are the three highest-value African cider flavourings because they are widely available, culturally recognisable and carry premium pricing in urban and export markets.

  • Ginger: 10â20 g/L fresh grated ginger added at secondary fermentation. Provides heat, aids preservation through gingerol antimicrobial action. Pairs best with dry apple base.
  • Hibiscus (roselle): 5â10 g/L dried calyces steeped in warm juice before fermentation or added as a tea at bottling. Delivers deep red colour, tartness and vitamin C. Popular in West African and East African markets.
  • Baobab: 15â30 g/L baobab fruit powder added post-fermentation. High vitamin C and pectin â use fining agents (bentonite or kieselsol/chitosan) to clarify. Adds citrus-creamy notes and strong health positioning for premium retail.

Always add flavourings after primary fermentation if you want to preserve aroma, and always stabilise with potassium sorbate (200 mg/L) plus potassium metabisulphite (50 mg/L free SOâ target) before sweetening or adding sugar-based flavour extracts.

Preventing Oxidation and Spoilage in Hot Weather

Heat accelerates every spoilage pathway: acetobacter turns cider to vinegar, wild yeasts create off-flavours, and oxygen drives browning and cardboard notes. The following controls are non-negotiable in tropical production.

  • Minimise headspace in every vessel and bottle â target less than 2 cm ullage.
  • Purge with COâ if available; otherwise fill from the bottom of the bottle using a bottling wand.
  • Keep free SOâ at 30â50 mg/L throughout storage.
  • Store in dark, ventilated rooms. Black plastic sheeting over windows is cheap and effective.
  • Never store near diesel, paint or strong-smelling chemicals â cider absorbs odours through closures.
  • Use crown caps or swing-tops with intact gaskets; cork is risky in low-humidity hot climates.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Source fruit at correct Brix (11â14 Â°Bx) and reject any fruit with visible rot or mould.
  2. Sanitise all equipment with no-rinse acid sanitiser or 1% sodium metabisulphite solution before every batch.
  3. Adjust juice pH to 3.2â3.8 and Brix to 11â14 before pitching yeast.
  4. Pitch a heat-tolerant yeast strain (EC-1118 or SafCider) at 1 g/L and maintain 18â24Â°C.
  5. Confirm fermentation is complete with stable gravity over 3 consecutive days before bottling.
  6. Prime with 4â8 g/L sugar depending on ambient temperature; never exceed 8 g/L above 28Â°C.
  7. Bottle in pressure-rated glass, wear eye protection, and condition in closed crates at 18â22Â°C.
  8. Store finished cider at 12â18Â°C, out of sunlight, with clear batch labels showing bottling date and ABV.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Small-Scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing (free full text)
  • Institute of Food Science & Technology â Cider Production Information Statement
  • Fermentis â SafCider Technical Brochure (PDF)
  • Lallemand â Lalvin EC-1118 Yeast Technical Data
  • South African Apple and Pear Producers' Association â Industry Resources

quiz.q: Which apple variety is recommended for highland areas in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Anna is a low-chill variety that grows well in African highlands.

quiz.q: What is the ideal ratio of sweet, tart, and bitter fruits for cider?
quiz.explanation: A 60/30/10 ratio balances sugar, acidity, and tannins for good cider.

quiz.q: How many kilograms of fruit are needed for a 20-liter batch of cider?
quiz.explanation: About 15-20 kg of fruit yields 12-15 liters of juice, enough for 20 liters after dilution or blending.

quiz.q: What is a cheap alternative to a commercial fruit press?
quiz.explanation: A DIY press using a car jack is affordable and effective.

quiz.q: How much juice can you expect from 20 kg of apples?
quiz.explanation: Apples yield about 60-75% juice by weight, so 20 kg gives roughly 12-15 liters.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding a campden tablet before fermentation?
options: B) To kill wild yeast and bacteria
quiz.explanation: Campden tablets release sulfites that inhibit wild microbes.

quiz.q: Which yeast is best for a dry cider?
quiz.explanation: Champagne yeast ferments all sugars, resulting in a dry cider.

quiz.q: What is the ideal starting gravity for cider?
quiz.explanation: This range provides enough sugar for fermentation without stressing yeast.

quiz.q: How much yeast nutrient is recommended per 4 liters?
quiz.explanation: 1 teaspoon per 4 liters helps prevent stuck fermentation.

quiz.q: What is the ideal fermentation temperature for cider?
quiz.explanation: 18-24Â°C is the optimal range for most cider yeasts.

quiz.q: How can you stop fermentation to keep cider sweet?
options: B) Cold crash and add sorbate
quiz.explanation: Cold crashing and potassium sorbate stabilize the cider and prevent refermentation.

quiz.q: What is racking?
quiz.explanation: Racking transfers cider off sediment to clarify it.

quiz.q: How long should secondary fermentation last?
quiz.explanation: 2-4 weeks allows for clarification and flavor development.

quiz.q: How much priming sugar is needed per liter for bottle carbonation?
quiz.explanation: 7-10 grams per liter gives good carbonation without bottle bombs.

quiz.q: What is a sign of over-carbonation in bottles?
quiz.explanation: Too much sugar can cause bottles to explode.

quiz.q: Which flavoring agent adds a deep red color to cider?
quiz.explanation: Hibiscus (zobo) petals impart a red color and tart flavor.

quiz.q: How much fresh ginger is recommended per 20 liters for ginger cider?
quiz.explanation: 50-100 grams of grated ginger gives a noticeable but not overwhelming spice.

quiz.q: When should you add hibiscus to cider?
quiz.explanation: Hibiscus can inhibit yeast, so add after fermentation.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using baobab powder in cider?
quiz.explanation: Baobab is rich in vitamin C and adds a tangy flavor.

quiz.q: How can you make a flavor extract for cider?
quiz.explanation: Steeping in vodka extracts flavors without dilution or contamination.

quiz.q: What causes oxidation in cider?
quiz.explanation: Oxygen reacts with cider compounds, causing stale flavors.

quiz.q: How can you minimize oxygen exposure during racking?
options: B) Use a siphon hose to the bottom
quiz.explanation: Siphoning gently to the bottom reduces splashing and oxygen pickup.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sanitizer concentration for bleach?
quiz.explanation: 1 tablespoon per 4 liters is effective and requires rinsing.

quiz.q: Why is temperature control important in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: High temperatures can produce off-flavors and fusel alcohols.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mold on your cider?
quiz.explanation: Mold indicates spoilage and can be toxic; discard the batch.

quiz.q: What is a sign of vinegar flies?
quiz.explanation: Vinegar flies indicate acetobacter infection, leading to vinegar.

quiz.q: How can you store cider in hot climates without a cellar?
options: C) In a cool box with ice
quiz.explanation: All these methods help keep cider cool and prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding potassium metabisulfite before bottling?
options: B) To prevent oxidation and refermentation
quiz.explanation: Metabisulfite releases SO2, which protects against oxidation and wild yeast.

quiz.q: How much potassium sorbate is used per 4 liters to stabilize cider?
quiz.explanation: 1/2 teaspoon per 4 liters inhibits yeast reproduction.

quiz.q: What is the best way to avoid spoilage in hot weather?
options: B) Sanitize everything and minimize oxygen
quiz.explanation: Sanitation and oxygen management are key to preventing spoilage.
